findings.reason: §2 (now §9's carried work) should extend `context_budget`'s predicate and `_backends.parse_events`/`classify_stream_failure` instead of hardcoding the refusal strings, so a dialect or context-budget change cannot leave the withheld-session check matching on a stale literal.
findings.text: `_session_too_large_to_continue` opens a run's stream itself (dispatch.py:11293-11321), iterates lines with `json.loads`, and hardcodes the context-refusal vocabulary `"Prompt is too long"` and `"blocking_limit"`. That vocabulary already has owners: `reckon/crew/context_budget.py:25` holds `_CONTEXT_REFUSAL_TEXT = "Prompt is too long"`, and `reckon/crew/recovery.py:4979` classifies `terminal_reason == "blocking_limit"`. The stream-line parsing it duplicates is owned by `reckon/_backends.py:parse_events` (3513) and the dialect-level classifiers `classify_stream_failure` (reckon/_backends.py:1096, 1367, 3798), which already expose the same event vocabulary. This is a census of the duplicated context-refusal vocabulary — the sites are `context_budget.py:25` (owner), `recovery.py:4979`, and the new `dispatch.py:11316-11321` — plus the duplicated `json.loads` stream loop at `dispatch.py:11287` against the owner `_backends.parse_events`.

rubric_items.deep_module: pass — the whole task-keyed continuation decision sits behind one entry point, `_task_session_resolution` (dispatch.py:11414), which hides selection (`_prior_same_task_run`), live-writer withholding (`_prior_session_still_held`) and harness ownership, delegating session resolution to the existing `resolve_session`. The interface is narrower than what it hides.
rubric_items.duplicate_owner: a finding — the context-refusal vocabulary is re-implemented in the plan's §2 code instead of extending its owner; owned by `reckon/crew/context_budget.py` (and the `blocking_limit` classifier at `reckon/crew/recovery.py:4979`).
rubric_items.interface_budget: pass — supplied counts public_definitions 1481, cli_options 317, mcp_views 33, refusal_families 23. The two remaining sections add to none of these: §7 flips `session_reuse` in the host and project layers without adding a definition, CLI option, MCP view or refusal family, and §9 is an ordering note that names no new surface. The landed sections account for what they retire rather than accreted surface: §2 removes the member-keyed resolver `_member_session_resolution`, and §3 retires the four roster session fields (`session_id`, `session_model`, `sessions`, `session_owners`) from the member schema.
rubric_items.reuse_search: pass — §1 is itself the reuse search (a 34-row map of every session-carry site with file:line, class and asserting tests; falsifier names `dispatch.py:3622-3634`, the redispatch `continued` branch, `crew resume`, `dispatch_review_for_run` and the reckon-ship Continuity rule), and §2 extends the existing dispatch decision in `reckon/crew/dispatch.py` (`_task_session_resolution`, dispatch.py:11414, delegating to `reckon/crew/resumption.py:resolve_session`) rather than forking a parallel resolver.
rubric_items.thin_wrapper: pass — the plan added no thin layer over existing machinery: §2 removed the member-keyed resolver `_member_session_resolution` instead of wrapping it, §3 retires the roster session fields, §7 is a one-line `session_reuse` configuration flip, and §9 adds no code. There is no new wrapper needing a justification.
